stem: A client is being switched from one opioid to another. Which principle is safest when using an equianalgesic conversion estimate?

options.A: Use the calculated equianalgesic dose without reduction because conversion factors fully account for cross-tolerance and individual response.
options.B: Increase the calculated dose of the new opioid because incomplete cross-tolerance makes the replacement opioid predictably less potent.
options.C: Treat the conversion as an estimate and generally start the new opioid below the calculated equivalent dose when appropriate because cross-tolerance and individual response vary.
options.D: Match the number and strength of tablets between opioids because equianalgesic estimates are unnecessary when both drugs are oral.

rationale: CDC states that equianalgesic/MME conversions are estimates and do not account for individual variability. The CDC table cautions not to use the calculated MME dose directly to determine the dose of a new opioid; the new opioid is typically dosed substantially lower to reduce overdose risk from incomplete cross-tolerance and variability. C is therefore the safest principle.
educational_objective: Use opioid equianalgesic conversions as estimates rather than exact switch doses and reduce the starting dose of the new opioid as clinically appropriate to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and patient variability.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022
source_version_date: November 4, 2022; current CDC guideline live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: MME conversion table cautions: equianalgesic conversions are estimates; do not use calculated MME dose directly when converting opioids; the new opioid is typically dosed substantially lower because of incomplete cross-tolerance and individual pharmacokinetic variability. Implementation considerations also advise reducing total daily dosage when changing opioids to account for incomplete cross-tolerance.
source_claim_supported: Opioid conversion estimates are not exact switch doses; the new opioid should generally be started below the calculated equivalent dose when clinically appropriate because incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variability increase overdose risk.

source_original.stem: A client is being switched from one opioid to another. Which principle is safest when using an equianalgesic conversion estimate?

options.A: Use the calculated equianalgesic dose without reduction because published conversion factors account completely for cross-tolerance and individual response.
options.B: Increase the calculated dose of the new opioid because incomplete cross-tolerance makes the replacement opioid predictably less potent.
options.C: Use the equianalgesic calculation as an estimate and generally begin the new opioid below the calculated dose when appropriate because cross-tolerance and patient response vary.
options.D: Match the number and strength of tablets between opioids because equianalgesic estimates are unnecessary when both medications are given orally.

source_original.rationale: CDC cautions that opioid conversion factors are estimates and should not be used as exact dosing equivalents for switching. A lower starting dose of the new opioid is generally used to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and variability.
source_original.source_detail: Recommendation 3 > Implementation Considerations; cautions regarding opioid conversion and equianalgesic estimates. CDC MMWR 2022 guideline; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Overview of Content — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12: medication administration, controlled substances, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the opioid-conversion construct and key C, corrected the source locator to the CDC MME table cautions plus relevant implementation text, tightened wording to avoid presenting conversions as exact, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: CDC 2022 opioid prescribing guideline; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: CDC guideline remains current and was live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: CDC MME conversion table cautions and opioid-switch implementation considerations
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately distinguishes estimation from exact dosing and retains the incomplete-cross-tolerance overdose-safety principle.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because conversion factors do not fully account for individual variability or cross-tolerance.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because dose escalation rather than reduction increases overdose risk.
distractor_audit.C: Correct and directly supported by CDC cautions.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because tablet counts/strengths are not interchangeable measures of opioid potency.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C incorporates both estimation uncertainty and dose-reduction safety.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are switch-dosing principles of comparable length and specificity.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — controlled-substance dosing and adverse-event prevention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the CDC conversion cautions and implementation text, all choices, rationale, objective and blueprint mapping. C remained uniquely correct.
